title: Fourier Analysis of Periodic Waves
short_intro: Fourier analysis is a mathematical framework that decomposes any arbitrary periodic waveform into a convergent infinite sum of harmonically related sines and cosines. It forms the foundation for understanding complex vibrations in continuous media, acoustics, and signal processing.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of average values, basic trigonometric Fourier coefficients for simple waveforms like square and triangular waves, orthogonality of trigonometric functions, and fundamental harmonic identification.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Complex exponential form of Fourier series, Dirichlet's conditions for convergence, Parseval's identity for power spectrum analysis, and Fourier transforms for non-periodic continuous waves.

prerequisites: Orthogonality relations of sine and cosine functions over a complete period
Definite integration techniques involving trigonometric identities

concept_notes.heading: Dirichlet's Conditions for Convergence
bullets: A periodic function f(t) with period T can be represented by a Fourier series if it satisfies specific mathematical constraints.
The function must be single-valued, continuous, or have a finite number of finite discontinuities within any one period.
The function must have a finite number of maxima and minima within the period T and be absolutely integrable.

concept_notes.heading: Trigonometric Fourier Series Expansion
bullets: Any periodic function f(t) of period T = 2π/ω can be expressed as an infinite series containing a constant term, fundamental frequencies, and integer multiples (harmonics).
The presence of even or odd symmetries in f(t) simplifies the series by systematically eliminating sine or cosine terms.
The constant term a<sub>0</sub> represents the direct current (DC) or average value of the waveform over one complete period.

concept_notes.heading: Harmonic Content and Waveform Symmetry
bullets: Even symmetry, defined by f(-t) = f(t), yields only cosine terms and a<sub>0</sub>, meaning all b<sub>n</sub> coefficients are zero.
Odd symmetry, defined by f(-t) = -f(t), yields only sine terms, meaning all a<sub>n</sub> and a<sub>0</sub> coefficients are zero.
Half-wave symmetry, defined by f(t ± T/2) = -f(t), ensures that the Fourier expansion contains only odd harmonics.

concept_notes.heading: Parseval's Theorem for Power Spectra
bullets: Parseval's theorem relates the total average power of a periodic signal to the sum of the powers contained in its individual harmonic components.
It states that the mean square value of a periodic function over a period equals the sum of the squares of the amplitudes of its Fourier components.
This theorem is essential for analyzing energy distribution across different frequency channels in oscillating systems.

derivations.title: Derivation of Fourier Coefficients
derivations.conditions: Function f(t) is periodic with period T = 2π/ω and satisfies Dirichlet's conditions.
steps: Write the general trigonometric Fourier series: f(t) =  rac{a_0}{2} + sum_{n=1}^{infty} left( a_n cos(nomega t) + b_n sin(nomega t) ight).
Integrate both sides of the equation from -T/2 to T/2 over one complete period to isolate a<sub>0</sub>, utilizing the orthogonality of sines and cosines.
To find a<sub>n</sub>, multiply both sides by cos(momega t) and integrate over one period, using orthogonality relations int_{-T/2}^{T/2} cos(nomega t)cos(momega t) dt =  rac{T}{2}delta_{nm}.
To find b<sub>n</sub>, multiply both sides by sin(momega t) and integrate over one period, yielding the integral expression for b<sub>n</sub>.
derivations.result: a_0 =  rac{2}{T} int_{-T/2}^{T/2} f(t) dt, quad a_n =  rac{2}{T} int_{-T/2}^{T/2} f(t) cos(nomega t) dt, quad b_n =  rac{2}{T} int_{-T/2}^{T/2} f(t) sin(nomega t) dt

derivations.title: Fourier Series of a Symmetric Square Wave
derivations.conditions: Square wave defined as f(t) = +V for 0 < t < T/2 and f(t) = -V for -T/2 < t < 0.
steps: Observe that the function is an odd function, meaning f(-t) = -f(t), which implies a_0 = 0 and all a_n = 0.
Set up the integral for the sine coefficients: b_n =  rac{2}{T} left[ int_{-T/2}^{0} (-V)sin(nomega t)dt + int_{0}^{T/2} Vsin(nomega t)dt ight].
Evaluate the integrals using int sin(nomega t) dt = - rac{cos(nomega t)}{nomega}.
Substitute the integration limits and simplify using ωT = 2π to get the final expression for b<sub>n</sub> in terms of n.
derivations.result: f(t) =  rac{4V}{pi} sum_{n=1,3,5...}^{infty}  rac{1}{n} sin(nomega t)

formula_sheet.name: General Trigonometric Fourier Series
formula_sheet.equation_html: f(t) =  rac{a_0}{2} + sum_{n=1}^{infty} left( a_n cos(nomega t) + b_n sin(nomega t) ight)
formula_sheet.variables: a_0, a_n, b_n = Fourier coefficients, omega = angular frequency

formula_sheet.name: DC Component Coefficient
formula_sheet.variables: T = time period, f(t) = periodic function
formula_sheet.conditions: Integrated over any one complete period

formula_sheet.name: Cosine Coefficient
formula_sheet.equation_html: a_n =  rac{2}{T} int_{0}^{T} f(t) cos(nomega t) dt
formula_sheet.variables: n = harmonic integer, omega = fundamental frequency

formula_sheet.name: Sine Coefficient
formula_sheet.equation_html: b_n =  rac{2}{T} int_{0}^{T} f(t) sin(nomega t) dt
formula_sheet.variables: n = harmonic integer, omega = fundamental frequency

formula_sheet.name: Complex Exponential Fourier Series
formula_sheet.variables: C_n = complex Fourier coefficients, i = imaginary unit
formula_sheet.conditions: Alternative compact form for periodic signals

formula_sheet.name: Complex Coefficient Formula
formula_sheet.equation_html: C_n =  rac{1}{T} int_{0}^{T} f(t) e^{-inomega t} dt
formula_sheet.variables: C_n = complex amplitude of nth harmonic
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid for all integer n from -infty to +infty

formula_sheet.name: Parseval's Identity for Power
formula_sheet.variables: P_{avg} = mean square power over one period
formula_sheet.units: Square of the unit of f(t)
formula_sheet.conditions: Power signals with finite mean square value

formula_sheet.name: Triangular Wave Fourier Series
formula_sheet.equation_html: f(t) =  rac{8V}{pi^2} sum_{n=1,3,5...}^{infty}  rac{(-1)^{(n-1)/2}}{n^2} sin(nomega t)
formula_sheet.variables: V = peak amplitude of triangular wave
formula_sheet.conditions: Symmetrical triangular wave passing through origin

graphs_and_experiments.title: Frequency Spectrum of a Square Wave
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A discrete line spectrum plotting amplitude (4V/nπ) against frequency (nω), showing only odd harmonics dropping off as 1/n.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that a square wave is composed solely of the fundamental and odd harmonics with amplitudes inversely proportional to harmonic number.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual questions regarding harmonic content and relative amplitudes of square versus triangular waves.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Harmonic Synthesis of a Square Wave
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Superposition curves showing the resultant waveform building up from just the fundamental, then fundamental plus 3rd harmonic, up to 5th harmonic.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates Gibbs phenomenon at sharp discontinuities and visualizes how summing sinusoidal harmonics reconstructs a non-sinusoidal wave.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in theoretical MCQ items regarding the Gibbs phenomenon and waveform reconstruction.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Audio Frequency Analyzer Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Block diagram of an audio oscillator connected to a wave analyzer or Cathode Ray Oscilloscope displaying component frequency peaks.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Physically verifies that musical instruments and complex acoustic tones contain multiple harmonic frequencies superimposed on a fundamental pitch.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Relates to practical acoustics, timbre, and Fourier decomposition in experimental physics setups.

solved_numericals.question: Find the constant term a_0 of a periodic function defined as f(t) = t for 0 < t < 2π, with period T = 2π.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for the DC coefficient: a_0 =  rac{2}{T} int_{0}^{T} f(t) dt.
Substitute T = 2π and f(t) = t into the integral: a_0 =  rac{2}{2pi} int_{0}^{2pi} t dt.
Evaluate the integral: int_{0}^{2pi} t dt = left[  rac{t^2}{2} ight]_{0}^{2pi} =  rac{4pi^2}{2} = 2pi.
Multiply by the outer factor: a_0 =  rac{1}{pi} (2pi) = 2.

solved_numericals.question: Determine whether the function f(t) = t^3 cos(t) contains sine or cosine terms in its Fourier series expansion over a symmetric interval about the origin.
solution_steps: Test for symmetry by replacing t with -t: f(-t) = (-t)^3 cos(-t).
Use trigonometric and algebraic properties: (-t)^3 = -t^3 and cos(-t) = cos(t).
Since f(-t) = -f(t), the function is an odd function, which means its Fourier expansion contains exclusively sine terms (a_0 = 0, a_n = 0).
solved_numericals.answer:
Only sine terms (b_n 
eq 0, a_0 = 0, a_n = 0)

solved_numericals.question: Using Parseval's identity, calculate the sum of the series sum_{n=1,3,5...}^{infty}  rac{1}{n^2} given that the root-mean-square value of a symmetric square wave of amplitude V is V.
solution_steps: Write Parseval's identity for the square wave:  rac{1}{T} int_{0}^{T} [f(t)]^2 dt =  rac{a_0^2}{4} +  rac{1}{2} sum_{n=1,3...}^{infty} (a_n^2 + b_n^2).
For a symmetric square wave, a_0 = 0, a_n = 0, and b_n =  rac{4V}{npi}.
Substitute the RMS value squared on the left side:  rac{1}{T} int_{0}^{T} [f(t)]^2 dt = V^2.
Substitute b_n into the right side: V^2 =  rac{1}{2} sum_{n=1,3...}^{infty} left( rac{4V}{npi}ight)^2 =  rac{1}{2}  rac{16V^2}{pi^2} sum_{n=1,3...}^{infty}  rac{1}{n^2}.
Simplify and solve for the target sum: sum_{n=1,3...}^{infty}  rac{1}{n^2} =  rac{V^2 pi^2}{8 V^2} =  rac{pi^2}{8}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: The function under analysis is strictly periodic with a well-defined, constant time period T.
Limitation: Fourier series cannot represent transient or non-periodic signals directly; such signals require the Fourier Integral Transform instead.
Limitation: Sharp discontinuities in waveforms lead to the Gibbs phenomenon, where finite partial sums overshoot the true value by approximately 9% near the jump.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Fourier series can only be applied to continuous sinusoidal waves.
common_misconceptions.correct: Fourier series can decompose any piecewise continuous, periodic waveform, including square, sawtooth, and triangular waves.
common_misconceptions.why: The basis functions are sines and cosines, but their linear superposition can model abrupt changes and non-sinusoidal profiles.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An even function contains both sine and cosine terms.
common_misconceptions.correct: An even function contains only cosine terms and the DC constant term a_0.
common_misconceptions.why: Sine functions are odd functions; integrating an even function multiplied by an odd function over a symmetric interval yields zero.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The number of harmonics required to reconstruct a wave is always infinite in practical physical systems.
common_misconceptions.correct: Band-limited physical systems act as low-pass filters, effectively eliminating high-frequency harmonics above a cutoff threshold.
common_misconceptions.why: Real physical media and instruments have inertia and damping that prevent the propagation of infinitely high frequencies.

quick_revision: Fourier analysis breaks down periodic waves into fundamental and harmonic sine/cosine components.
Dirichlet's conditions ensure the existence and convergence of the Fourier series.
Even functions yield only cosine terms (a_n); odd functions yield only sine terms (b_n).
Square waves contain only odd harmonics with amplitudes proportional to 1/n.
Triangular waves contain only odd harmonics with amplitudes proportional to 1/n^2.
Parseval's theorem equates total signal power to the sum of powers in its harmonic components.
The Gibbs phenomenon causes a 9% overshoot near sharp discontinuities when using truncated Fourier series.
